entry.title: Rebuilding PAYDAY 3 Modding for Unreal Engine 5

link.title: Rebuilding PAYDAY 3 Modding for Unreal Engine 5

entry.content:
When PAYDAY 3 moved from Unreal Engine 4.27 to UE5 in August 2026, much of the community’s modding environment stopped being usable. Projects, generated definitions and packaging workflows had accumulated around the old engine. Moving to UE5 meant revisiting the assumptions underneath them.

I had already spent a substantial amount of time inside those constraints. Alongside VanillaHUD+, HUDCore and other mods, I had helped maintain the community’s earlier UE4 development project. I knew how much work could happen before a modder reached the part they actually wanted to build: inspect cooked assets, reconstruct dependencies, repair definitions, cook through separate tools, then copy files into the game.

Our initial aim was to recover that environment. Over a short, intensive period, it became a larger engineering project: a custom Unreal Editor, a Modkit built around installed game content, integrated authoring and packaging tools, and a runtime framework with its own in-game interface.

This article covers how those pieces fit together and the boundaries we are still working through. The portfolio case study provides a shorter visual overview.

From rebuilding to rethinking

Restoring the old workflow would have restored its friction too. In UE4, even a fairly focused modification could involve understanding several tools and maintaining a reconstructed version of the content it touched. Some categories, particularly materials and animations, were difficult because editor output and game expectations did not line up reliably.

The question became: could we make the editor understand more of the existing game, then carry a mod from creation to runtime through a consistent workflow?

I developed the custom UE5 compatibility editor, maintained the Modkit project, built CrimeForge for editor-side mod development, and rebuilt PDML for runtime integration. I also worked on Suzie integration, interfaces, templates and documentation. This remains a community project, with other developers contributing features, testing and guides. JMAP, Suzie, FModel, Unreal Engine and Wwise are existing projects that the toolchain builds upon.

  1. Custom UE5 EditorMount supported cooked game content
  2. PD3 ModkitAuthor content in the development project
  3. JMAP + SuzieResolve reflected native game types
  4. CrimeForgeCreate, validate, cook and package mods
  5. PDMLIntegrate plugin mods into the game

Installed game content and locally generated reflection data supply the editor. CrimeForge produces plugin mods for PDML.

Teaching an editor to load shipped content

A standard Unreal Editor expects editable source assets. PAYDAY 3 ships cooked packages prepared for its runtime. Those packages preserve what the game needs to execute and render, but do not retain the complete editor representation of every asset.

The custom editor is based on Unreal Engine 5.5.4, matching the game version targeted by the Modkit. Users configure their installed game directory and AES key, supply the current AssetRegistry.bin, and generate native reflection data. The engine mounts supported retail containers, including IoStore content. The external registry makes supported assets discoverable in the Content Browser under their original /Game/... locations.

Mounting a container is only the beginning. The editor also needs to resolve dependencies, understand the classes referenced by packages, and tolerate data that was serialized for a shipped game. My compatibility work spans cooked package loading, registry preservation during refreshes, cooked Blueprint references, thumbnails, supported level loading and unversioned property serialization.

The architectural choice is to use the user’s installed game as the content source. Base-game assets generally remain read-only references and dependencies. The Modkit is not a redistributed PAYDAY 3 source project, and it does not contain the original native implementation. Modders create their own assets and supported replacements separately.

That boundary is useful in practice. A creator can inspect an existing asset’s defaults and relationships without first recreating its entire surrounding project. It also keeps game-owned content external rather than turning each development checkout into a duplicate content library. The custom editor documentation describes the supported compatibility areas and local configuration.

Reconstructing the missing game types

An asset registry answers which assets exist. It cannot supply the native classes those assets depend on.

PAYDAY 3 content references game-specific types, properties and inheritance relationships that do not exist in ordinary Unreal Engine. A cooked Data Asset can be present and discoverable while still being unusable because its class is missing. Blueprint parents create the same problem.

The Modkit addresses this through a modified JMAP dumping workflow and Suzie. GenerateJmap.bat gathers reflection metadata from a locally running game and places the JMAP in Content/DynamicClasses/. At project startup, Suzie reads that metadata, generates native class representations and registers them for editor use. My work integrates and extends that workflow for PAYDAY 3 compatibility.

This makes reflected game classes available to supported assets and authoring workflows. Modders can reference game-specific Data Asset types and derive Blueprints from reconstructed native parents without manually maintaining an enormous collection of generated UHT stubs.

There is an essential limit: a reflected function signature does not contain its original C++ implementation. The editor can understand that a function or property exists without reproducing the behaviour behind it. Features requiring that behaviour need explicit implementations or appropriate runtime integration.

This also changes maintenance. After ordinary updates, users generally refresh the JMAP and AssetRegistry.bin, then restart the project so Suzie can regenerate local class data. Both inputs need to match the game build. It is more maintainable than treating generated definitions as permanent, although engine or serialization changes can still require code fixes. The reflected-types guide explains the two inputs separately.

Making cooked assets useful

Getting an asset to load is different from recovering an editable version. I have tried to keep that distinction clear in both the tooling and documentation.

For supported assets, the workflow is to inspect the cooked original, convert it to an uncooked copy or supported replacement, make the required changes, and include the result in the mod’s packaging configuration. Some simpler types can be reconstructed substantially. More complex assets may expose useful defaults, components and references alongside generated stubs or placeholder data.

Blueprints and widgets make the limitations especially visible. Cooked data generally cannot provide the original editor graphs. Reconstructing a class or widget hierarchy gives a creator a closer starting point, but it does not restore all of the original logic.

As a UI Engineer, this has been one of the most interesting areas. A game widget depends on more than its appearance. Its parent class, properties, named bindings, animations and tick-related class flags can all matter. Recovering the hierarchy while losing expected binding metadata can leave something that looks plausible but still needs additional work. Widget compatibility and more complete reconstruction remain ongoing.

Meshes, skeletons and animations provide another useful authoring path. Supported game skeletons can be used to preview custom animations, and the editor supports demonstrated static mesh, skeletal mesh and material workflows. Compatibility still varies by asset and build.

The team’s material baking work, credited to Columbus in the announcement, is another practical improvement. PAYDAY 3 materials can combine colour layers and masks that previously needed manual interpretation. Baking helps produce a more useful starting texture, although some materials still differ from their in-game appearance and accessory textures are not necessarily included.

Audio has its own dependencies. The Modkit includes a modified Wwise integration based on 2023.1.15.8789.3579; users supply matching Audiokinetic third-party SDK files. Compatible cooked audio workflows depend on that integration as well as the engine and reflection setup.

CrimeForge: designing around the modder’s task

Once the editor could expose useful game content, the surrounding workflow needed the same attention. I built CrimeForge as a custom editor plugin so creating, configuring and packaging a mod could happen through one interface.

The C++ and Slate manager centres on mod plugins. Searchable cards expose selection controls, icons, metadata and Forge actions. Clicking an icon opens the plugin’s content root. Information and configuration interfaces cover names, authors, descriptions, versions, links, dependencies and packaging settings.

Each mod has its own Unreal plugin namespace. That makes ownership easier to understand: the mod’s content is separate from mounted game references, while explicit replacement assets can still target original paths.

The three current templates are Blank, Logic Mod and Custom Heist. Blank creates the plugin and standard assets, including PAL_<ModName> and DA_<ModName>. Logic Mod adds a ModActorBase Blueprint and registers it. Custom Heist creates a PD3HeistDataAsset, a level such as LVL_<ModName>, and the initial registration and level-path references.

Those connections are repetitive but consequential. Automating them lets authors start with a coherent foundation. HUD and audio templates are planned additions. Compatible legacy UE4 or non-CrimeForge imports can also help migrate content, but conversion cannot guarantee that every older mod will work in UE5.

Validation is part of the interface design. CrimeForge checks Primary Asset Labels, Asset Manager registration, chunk configuration, explicit assets, dependencies and leftover template references before starting the longer cook. Errors block the operation; warnings identify conditions to review. Fix Issues repairs recognised configuration problems where safe, while references requiring an author’s decision remain visible.

Why Forge needs two cooking paths

Forge is the name of CrimeForge’s build operation. It validates a mod, resolves its packaging configuration, cooks the required content and produces a complete PDML-compatible plugin. The interesting difficulty is that a plugin’s own content and a base-game replacement do not share the same content root.

A mod containing only /MyMod/... assets can follow the plugin packaging path. A replacement for /Game/... must preserve the original package path so the game can resolve it as intended. Packaging only the plugin root does not solve that second case.

CrimeForge uses Primary Asset Labels and their Explicit Assets list to describe what belongs in a build. Chunk IDs need to avoid game and DLC values; the documentation recommends values above 100.

When external replacements are present, Forge performs a plugin cook and an additional project cook for the required replacement content, then combines the selected cooked output into the final plugin structure. Plugin-only mods skip the extra pass. This keeps the ordinary case simpler while accommodating mods that mix new content with replacements.

The public PackagePlugin automation also makes the second pass explicit through a packaging manifest. It records external cook packages and the expected chunk package set, validates their relationship, and rejects ambiguous input. That matters because mounted base-game dependencies should remain references rather than becoming an uncontrolled set of extra cook targets. The Forge documentation and automation source cover this boundary.

The pipeline uses Unreal Automation Tool and custom CrimeForge.Automation tooling, with preparation for missing or stale automation components. Output can include .pak, .utoc and .ucas containers, retained inside a complete plugin. Forge also produces a distribution archive and can copy the mod to the game and launch it for testing. Storefront-specific launching still needs additional validation.

PDML: carrying the workflow into the game

CrimeForge’s output needs a matching runtime contract. PDML is the loader and integration framework I rebuilt for UE5, now available in public early access.

Mods are installed as complete folders, for example PAYDAY3/Mods/MyMod/MyMod.uplugin. Keeping descriptors, cooked assets and supporting content together gives the loader a clear discovery boundary, separate from the game’s own Content/Paks/ directory. The Modkit includes PDML development assets so authors can reference its exposed Blueprint APIs.

PDML provides supported registration and initialization for Blueprint logic mods, UI, settings and custom-heist content. For players, its most visible parts are the main-menu Mod Manager and integrated settings. They can inspect installed compatible mods, read metadata and open download pages. Supported mods can expose their own configuration inside the game.

That combination builds on my HUDCore and VanillaHUD+ work. A common framework can reduce how much surrounding integration each HUD author needs to recreate. It does not automatically restore the original HUD’s widget logic.

Custom heists benefit from the same connection: inspect supported levels, author a new level using reflected classes and heist data, Forge it, then register it through PDML. This is a foundation for more accessible heist development. Advanced navigation, AirNav and some game-specific behaviours still need compatibility work.

The remaining runtime boundary

One ongoing challenge is controlled runtime plugin management through the SBZModloader subsystem work. Discovering a descriptor, mounting cooked containers and registering a content mount point do not automatically make every asset discoverable to the Asset Registry.

Startup-loaded plugins and plugins introduced after the game is running can take different paths. Resolving that involves plugin activation, registry data and runtime asset discovery together. I am treating this as ongoing engineering, not a claim that reliable dynamic mounting, unloading or hot-swapping already ships.

Load ordering, enable/disable controls and stronger dependency management remain planned or under consideration. ModWorkshop integration has been prototyped, but in-game browsing, downloads and updates are future work. Further additive inventory content is another direction, rather than a blanket promise of support for every new weapon, mask or outfit.

Documentation, feedback and recognition

The environment needs to be usable by people who did not build it. Our Antora and AsciiDoc documentation connects installation, FModel and Wwise setup, JMAP generation, editor configuration, templates, validation, replacement authoring and runtime testing. A beginner should have a repeatable route to a first mod without first learning every engine detail involved.

Community testing has helped expose unsupported assets, setup problems and storefront differences. The announcement’s contributor list credits Capcake, Pinki_Ninja, Columbus, DrProtogen, Braidy08 and Gordon Greedman across documentation, compatibility work and testing. FlamingFury1000 also contributed future interface concepts, which are separate from the current UI pictured here.

One of the most encouraging parts has been seeing Starbreeze acknowledge what we’ve been building. They’ve been positive about the work and have shown interest in supporting it further. I can’t share additional details at this stage, but having the game’s developers recognise the effort means a lot. This remains a community-developed toolchain.

Working across these systems has reinforced a practical lesson for me: compatibility needs to hold from inspection through packaging to runtime use. An asset appearing in the editor is only one milestone. Clear validation, understandable interfaces and good documentation are part of making that technical capability useful to someone else.

There is more to do on asset coverage, complex widget reconstruction, runtime discovery and custom-heist systems. The foundation now brings authoring, packaging and in-game integration much closer together. The goal is to give creators more time to build modifications that were previously difficult or impractical, and less time reconstructing the environment around them.

The Modkit repository, documentation and PDML release are available publicly. My earlier UE4 modding project and VanillaHUD+ article cover the work that led here.

All screenshots in this article come from the public community announcement. The social preview uses the banner from the PDML ModWorkshop page.
entry.summary: Building a custom UE5 compatibility editor, integrating reflected game types, and connecting CrimeForge's authoring pipeline to the PDML runtime framework.

entry.title: Building a Death Stranding 2-style Voxel 3D Map in Unreal Engine 5

link.title: Building a Death Stranding 2-style Voxel 3D Map in Unreal Engine 5

entry.content:
Earlier this year, Kojima Productions’ Ildar Valeev gave a GDC talk called “‘DEATH STRANDING 2’: Making of Voxel 3D UI Map”, walking through how the studio built the game’s map screen: capturing an open-world level, converting it into voxel data, and rendering it back out without any hand-placed artist assets, while staying fast and memory-efficient.

I wanted to see how far the same idea could go in our own UE5 project, for COLDLIGHT’s map screen. This post is the full technical breakdown of what that turned into - the pipeline, the performance work, and a whole category of bugs that only show up after a level save.

The development screenshots show my COLDLIGHT implementation. The three reference slides below are credited to Ildar Valeev and Kojima Productions’ GDC presentation and illustrate the approach that inspired it. A shorter overview is on the project page.

The high-level pipeline

The system splits cleanly into five phases, plus a UMG integration layer on top:

  1. Capture - sample the level from a grid of hemisphere and slice views, deduplicate into a voxel grid, and save the result to a self-describing binary file.
  2. Processing - a visibility flood-fill plus depth-based occluder culling, to discard geometry nothing can ever see.
  3. Packing - group surviving voxels into 4x4x4 blocks, each carrying Level-1 and Level-2 occupancy bitmasks and a render-data buffer.
  4. Chunking - group blocks by spatial region, with chunk-relative location indices instead of absolute ones.
  5. Rendering - bake it all into instanced meshes with a custom ray-box HLSL shader doing the actual per-voxel resolution.

On top of that, a UMG integration layer drives an isolated scene capture with a free-orbiting camera, feeding a map widget the player actually interacts with.

Capture: hemisphere + slice passes

The capture pass samples the level from two kinds of viewpoints - a hemisphere of directional views for broad coverage, and a grid of axis-aligned slice views to catch detail the hemisphere pass misses. Each capture reads depth and colour and unprojects the results into world-space points, which get deduplicated into a voxel grid as they come in.

One early bug here was subtle: SCS_DeviceDepth was quantizing depth reads just enough to introduce real error at range. Switching to SCS_SceneDepth with matrix-free unprojection fixed it outright.

The slice pass was also the single biggest performance win of the whole project, more on that below.

Processing: visibility and occluder culling

Two culling passes run after capture. A visibility flood-fill removes points that aren’t reachable from open space, and a depth-based occluder culling pass removes points that are provably behind solid geometry from every relevant direction.

The occluder culling pass went through a real redesign. The first version used a single top-down height map - “is there a higher point in this column?” - which works for most terrain but actively breaks on near-vertical geometry: a point on a cliff face can be the frontmost surface from a side-on view while still not being the topmost point in its column from directly above, so the height-map version was incorrectly stripping large sections of cliff faces. The fix was to make it properly six-directional (top, bottom, and all four horizontal axes), with a configurable minimum number of occluded directions required before a point gets culled. Visually confirmed fixed, and it still meaningfully culls genuinely buried geometry - roughly 20% of points removed post-fix, down from around 50% with the buggy version, at negligible extra cost (about 0.05s for all six directions on top of the existing pipeline).

Packing and chunking

Surviving points get packed into 4x4x4 voxel blocks. Each block stores a 24-bit location index plus two levels of occupancy bitmask - an 8-bit Level-1 mask for 2x2x2 sub-regions, and a 64-bit Level-2 mask for individual voxels - alongside a start index into a render-data buffer holding the actual per-voxel colour data. Blocks then get grouped into spatial chunks, with their location indices re-expressed relative to the chunk’s own local grid rather than the whole capture volume.

This is also where the project picked up its persistent Data Asset boundary: UVoxelMapDataAsset holds the packed chunk data plus the grid-context fields (capture center, grid origin, block world size, and so on) needed to decode block positions back into world space later. Without those fields traveling with the chunks, the packed data alone can’t be turned back into anything meaningful.

Rendering: ray-box voxel shader

Each block becomes one instance on a UHierarchicalInstancedStaticMeshComponent, billboarded and driven by custom material logic doing 4x4x4 DDA stepping through the block’s own occupancy bitmasks - resolving real per-voxel colour and depth per hit, not just showing a flat billboard. Distance-based LOD skips the full per-voxel stepping past a configurable threshold and falls back to a single representative colour for the block, with a dithered transition band instead of a hard pop.

Per-voxel colour data is baked into a runtime lookup texture - one texel per captured voxel - wrapped across a fixed row width rather than using one unbounded row, since a single-row texture wide enough for a large multi-segment capture would blow straight past texture dimension limits.

Getting to production scale

At real scale (a capture volume broken into 4000-unit segments, 64-unit voxels, 128 render resolution), the pipeline needed real performance work, all confirmed against real before/after timing:

  • The slice pass was oversampling 4-8x relative to what the geometry actually needed. Tuning slice count and spacing cut slice-pass time roughly 5x, for under 3% coverage loss.
  • ParallelFor on both the per-pixel capture loop and the per-voxel culling loops.
  • The visibility flood-fill was rewritten from TSet/TMap hash lookups to dense TBitArray grids, O(1) indexing instead of hashing, for a 23x speedup on its own.
  • A per-view line-trace pre-check skips slice views aimed at open air before doing any real capture work.

Altogether, a full per-segment pipeline (hemisphere + slice + visibility filter + occluder culling) went from multiple minutes per segment down to about 1.35 seconds, roughly a 175x improvement end to end. An async, pipelined GPU-readback rewrite was attempted for the slice pass specifically, but hit a genuine runtime hang and got abandoned in favor of the sampling-density fix, which solved the actual problem without the risk of touching RHI-level code.

The instance-count wall: 673K instances and the editor freeze

Once real levels started producing 600K+ voxel block instances, selecting the render actor at all (in the outliner or the viewport) froze the editor solid. This turned out to be two separate problems wearing the same disguise:

  • Unreal’s per-instance selection outline system tries to draw a highlight around every single instance when an ISM/HISM component gets selected. At this scale that’s catastrophically expensive, and there’s no legitimate reason to ever select this component by hand: it’s a pure rendering proxy for already-baked data. Setting bSelectable = false on the component removes it from the selection system entirely.
  • Separately, AddInstanceComponent (needed so the runtime-created component actually saves with the level) implicitly sets RF_Transactional, which means Unreal’s undo/transaction system may snapshot the entire instance transform and custom-data array on any transactable operation that touches the component, a much larger cost than the Details-panel display itself, and the more likely real cause of the original freeze. Clearing RF_Transactional after adding the component keeps it saving with the level while excluding it from that snapshotting specifically.

Splitting capture from render

The system started as a single actor doing both authoring-time capture and runtime display. That got split into two: AVoxelMapCaptureActor (capture, processing, packing, chunking - produces a Data Asset, and is only ever needed transiently during a bake) and AVoxelMapRenderActor (consumes already-packed chunk data, builds the renderable instances, and drives the UI’s orbit-camera scene capture - the thing that actually needs to exist in a shipped level). Shared structs and stateless utility functions (packed block/chunk data, the world-position decode function, a couple of bit-manipulation helpers) moved into a common shared module both actors use identically.

This also meant building real editor tooling: a “Build Voxel 3D World” pipeline that spawns a capture actor from a set of project-wide default settings, auto-fits its capture bounds to the level, runs the full segmented capture, converts the result into a Data Asset in the level’s own content folder, then spawns and configures a render actor pointed at it, registered as a proper custom build type through Unreal’s own build system, so it shows up in the native Build menu alongside the engine’s own build steps, with a progress dialog and cancel support.

UI integration: orbit camera and markers

The map itself renders through an isolated SceneCaptureComponent2D restricted to a show-only list containing just the voxel block mesh: nothing else in the level bleeds into the capture. An orbit camera (yaw, pitch, zoom, pan, all independently clamped) feeds that capture, driven by mouse-drag and scroll input in a UMG widget.

The player’s own representation on the map ended up as two deliberately separate systems, rather than one:

  • A 3D player model: a mesh placed directly in the voxel scene at the player’s real-world position, baked into the same scene capture as the voxel blocks. Since block instances are already placed at true absolute world-space positions, the player’s actual location drops straight in with no coordinate remapping needed.
  • A set of 2D UI markers: player location, points of interest, objectives, and whatever else comes later, rendered as icons directly in the UMG widget, entirely independent of the 3D scene. Since these markers live in screen space, they need a live projection from world position through the map camera’s actual current view (its live transform and field of view) into normalized screen coordinates, not the player’s own camera, which is a different view entirely. That projection recomputes on every camera move, so markers track correctly through rotate, zoom, and pan, not just on initial placement.

Keeping those two systems independent means a marker can exist without a 3D model and vice versa, and neither has to know anything about how the other is implemented.
entry.summary: How I built a fully procedural, artist-asset-free 3D voxel map for COLDLIGHT's map screen - hemisphere capture, occluder culling, a 673K-instance editor freeze, and the save/reload bugs that came with it.

entry.title: Building Easy Icon Font: Fonts, COLR Glyphs, and the Bug That Made Every Icon Render Twice

link.title: Building Easy Icon Font: Fonts, COLR Glyphs, and the Bug That Made Every Icon Render Twice

entry.content:
I didn’t set out to build a font engineering tool. I set out to stop tabbing over to an external website every time I needed a new icon in my UI font. One afternoon of that friction was enough - so instead of opening yet another browser tab, I spent a day building an in-editor tool for Unreal that does the conversion itself. That day turned into a proper plugin, a custom Slate editor window, a Python font-building backend, and - because nothing in engine tooling is ever as simple as it first looks - a multi-day chase after a bug that made color icons render as ghostly double exposures of themselves.

Why fonts for icons at all

The pitch is simple: an icon baked into a font behaves like a character. It inherits the color of the surrounding text for free. It scales to any size with zero blur, because it’s a vector outline, not a bitmap. And it drops straight into rich text - <icon id="icon_bell"/> sits inline with a sentence the same way a letter does, no manual placement code required.

The honest tradeoff is that a texture atlas is simpler, more predictable in memory, and doesn’t need any of the font-table machinery a glyph does. I don’t think icon fonts are a universal answer - for a fixed icon grid like a HUD or inventory screen, an atlas is probably the better call. But for icons that need to sit inline with text at arbitrary sizes, or that need to stay pixel-sharp at every zoom level a UI might throw at them, a font earns its keep. So the plugin ended up supporting both: build a glyph when it makes sense, fall back to a texture when it doesn’t.

Three ways to bake an icon

Not every icon source is the same kind of problem, so the tool auto-detects which of three representations actually fits:

  • Mono-vector - a single flat-color SVG, extruded directly into a real glyf outline. Infinitely scalable, tinted by whatever text color it’s displayed with, exactly like a letter.
  • Color-vector - flat, limited-palette raster art (or multi-fill SVG), quantized down to a small palette, traced region by region, and rebuilt as a multi-layer COLR/CPAL glyph. Still a true vector outline underneath - the color is just baked in rather than inherited.
  • Texture fallback - anything that doesn’t vectorize cleanly (gradients, photographic detail) just becomes a plain UTexture2D, no font involved.

The mono-vector path was the easy part - parse the SVG path data, walk the contours, hand them to a TTGlyphPen, done. Getting even-odd SVG fill rules to survive the trip into TrueType’s nonzero winding rule needed some care (a shape with a hole, like a letter “O” traced from a gear icon, needs its inner contour wound the opposite direction from its outer one, or the hole just fills solid) - but that was a solvable, well-understood problem.

Color-vector was where things got interesting.

Proving COLR actually worked before building on it

COLR/CPAL - the OpenType extension that lets a single glyph be built from multiple colored outline layers stacked on top of each other - isn’t something every font renderer supports. Rather than build a whole quantize-and-trace pipeline on a hopeful assumption, I hand-built a tiny two-layer test font first: a red square behind a blue triangle, nothing else. Dropped it straight into a UMG Text Block in the editor.

It rendered in color, correctly layered. That one test was worth more than any amount of documentation-reading - it confirmed Slate’s FreeType build genuinely reads COLR data, not just glyf, before I sank real time into the segmentation and tracing logic on top of it.

The bug that made icons render twice

Once the real pipeline was built - PIL for quantization, scikit-image for contour tracing, fontTools for assembling the layers - I fed it a badge icon: a navy ring, a blue circle inside it, a gold star on top. Three flat colors, nested regions, a reasonable real-world test case.

What came back looked like a double exposure. The ring showed up as an uneven crescent instead of a clean circle. The star had a ghost copy of itself offset diagonally, like the whole icon had been photographed through a slightly misaligned second lens.

My first theory was a seam problem - each color traced independently, so maybe the boundary between two adjacent colors was getting simplified slightly differently on each side, leaving a sliver of a gap. I added mask dilation to make adjacent layers overlap instead of almost-touch. No change. Same ghosting, pixel-for-pixel identical to before.

That result was actually the useful part - it meant the bug wasn’t in the boundary between colors, since a boundary fix had done nothing. I built a small standalone renderer to composite the layers by hand and inspect the raw glyph coordinates directly, bypassing every layer of assumption in between. And there it was: each color layer’s xMin didn’t match its hmtx left-side-bearing. I’d hardcoded every layer’s bearing to zero, but TTGlyphPen-built glyphs don’t have their bounds populated at build time - and a font renderer uses the mismatch between a glyph’s declared bearing and its actual outline position to shift the glyph horizontally. Every layer was getting shifted by a different, wrong amount, because every layer’s shape sat at a different true position and I’d told the renderer to pretend they all started at zero.

The fix was small once found - compute the real bearing from each layer’s own geometry instead of assuming zero - but finding it meant ruling out two entire categories of plausible-sounding explanations first. The dilation attempt wasn’t wasted, either; it’s still in the pipeline today as a genuine safety margin against seam gaps, it just wasn’t this bug.

Don’t ship the file people are actively editing

Somewhere in testing, icons that had worked days earlier started rendering as the classic Windows “tofu” placeholder - the black box with PRIVATE USE stamped on it that shows up when a codepoint can’t resolve to a real glyph. The font file itself turned out to be fine. The actual problem was upstream of the font entirely: every plugin update I’d shipped included the live, working font file as part of the package. Extracting a new zip over an existing install silently overwrote whatever icons had already been built - there was no warning, no conflict prompt, just a quiet reset back to the shipped version.

The fix became a small architectural rule: never ship the file a user is actively editing. The plugin now ships a blank template font that’s safe to overwrite on every update, and a one-time Setup step clones it into the real working file only if that file doesn’t already exist. Simple in hindsight, but it took losing test data to actually notice the update process was destructive in the first place.

Supporting six engine versions is its own project

Once the plugin worked, “does it work” turned out to have a much longer tail than expected. Building across Unreal 5.1 through 5.8 surfaced a small museum of version-specific problems: an FString factory method that didn’t exist yet in 5.1, a UPROPERTY category rule that’s only enforced under Engine-module packaging (never during normal project compiles, so it stayed invisible until the first real distribution build), a FJsonObject internal type that changed between engine releases, an MSVC toolset UE 5.2 specifically wasn’t validated against, an Android NDK mismatch on 5.1. None of these were bugs in the plugin’s own logic - each one was a real API or toolchain difference that only a genuine build against that specific engine version would ever catch.

That eventually justified building a second piece of tooling alongside the plugin itself: a PowerShell script that builds, tests, and packages against every supported engine version in one pass, with a live dashboard and a final report listing the actual warning and error lines per version - not just a pass/fail count. Getting that script running reliably turned into its own small debugging arc, including a genuinely memorable one: .ps1 files need a UTF-8 byte-order mark for Windows PowerShell to read certain characters correctly, and losing that one invisible marker was enough to make an otherwise-correct script throw parser errors on lines that had nothing wrong with them at all.

Where it landed

The finished plugin is a custom Slate editor window - not a Blueprint utility widget, an actual native tool - with a live preview bar reading straight from the font file, a dependency status light, one-click Setup, and automatic DataTable syncing so the DataTable powering the icon lookup never drifts out of sync with the font itself. A rich text decorator lets icons sit inline with prose, with per-instance size and color overrides. Full Doxygen documentation covers setup, the widget and rich-text reference, and troubleshooting for the handful of failure modes real usage actually turned up.

It’s on Fab now, still under active iteration - the SVG-native color-vector path (skipping the raster round-trip entirely for icons that started as multi-color SVGs) is the next thing on the list.
entry.summary: How an in-editor Unreal tool for baking PNG/SVG icons into real font glyphs turned into mono-vector outlines, multi-layer COLR/CPAL color glyphs, a double-exposure rendering bug, and shipping across six engine versions.

entry.title: Building the Mover Cover System
entry.content:
Cover mechanics are one of those systems that look deceptively simple from the outside. Press a button, character hugs a wall, duck behind it. But building one that works robustly across rotated geometry, network prediction, concave corners, and Mover’s experimental movement architecture turned out to be one of the deeper technical problems I’ve worked on.

This is a writeup on how I built the Mover Cover System - a C++ plugin that adds a full cover gameplay system to any Mover-based character with a single actor component.

Why Mover?

Epic’s Mover plugin is a ground-up rewrite of the character movement system, designed to be modular, network-prediction-aware, and simulation-driven. It’s still marked experimental, but it’s clearly the direction UE5 is heading, and building on it early means everything the plugin does is designed for the future of Unreal movement - not bolted onto legacy UCharacterMovementComponent assumptions.

The tradeoff is that Mover has almost no third-party ecosystem yet. If you want a cover system, you build it yourself.

Architecture

The plugin has three layers:

UMoverCoverComponent - an actor component you drop onto your character. It owns all the cover detection traces, wall tracking, edge/corner detection, and gap scanning. It also manages the input widget prompts and the FCoverModeInputs struct that feeds the simulation.

UCoverWalkingMode - a Mover movement mode registered on the CharacterMoverComponent. It derives from UWalkingMode so floor detection, gravity, and collision all work normally. The only override is GenerateMove_Implementation, which replaces the player’s directional input with cover-locked lateral movement, wall depth correction, edge peeking, and corner transition driving.

FCoverModeInputs - a custom Mover input struct that carries all cover state through the simulation. Wall normals, locations, corner data, gap data, flags for every state. This struct is NetSerialized so both client and server read the same data and make the same movement decisions at the same simulation tick.

Mode transitions (UCoverEntryTransition, UCoverExitTransition) are wired onto the Walking and Cover modes respectively. Rather than calling QueueNextMode directly from game-thread code, the transitions read bShouldBeInCoverMode from FCoverModeInputs each simulation tick and fire when the flag changes. This means mode switching happens inside Mover’s prediction system - not outside it - which is the difference between multiplayer that works and multiplayer that desynchs.

Wall Detection and Classification

Entering cover fires a sphere sweep from the character’s forward vector. On hit, it runs a secondary horizontal trace at head height toward the wall to classify the surface:

  • Full cover - wall blocks the head-height trace. Character stands.
  • Half cover - wall doesn’t reach head height. Character crouches.

This classification reruns every tick during UpdateCoverWall so it updates dynamically as the character shimmies along surfaces of varying height - useful for walls that transition from full to half mid-length.

A wall depth tracking sweep fires each tick to keep the character snapped to the surface. Wall normals and tangents are recomputed each tick so shimmying across rotated or diagonal geometry stays stable.

The Quaternion Bug

Early on, the character would spin erratically when against walls rotated on the yaw - a 40-degree wall, for example. The debug output showed a normal like (-0.64, -0.77, 0) and the angular velocity flipping sign every other frame.

The cause: ToRotationVector() on a quaternion is unstable near the 180-degree singularity. When the desired facing is just over 180 degrees from the current facing, the rotation vector flips direction frame to frame, producing the spin.

The fix is one line:

if (ToFacing.W < 0.0f)
{
    ToFacing = FQuat(-ToFacing.X, -ToFacing.Y, -ToFacing.Z, -ToFacing.W);
}

Negating all four components gives the mathematically identical rotation via the shorter arc. q and -q represent the same orientation - this just ensures we always take the path under 180 degrees.

Corners and Gaps

Outside corners are detected with an L-shaped probe: a lookahead trace in the shimmy direction, then from the end of that trace, a second trace in the reverse direction looking for a connecting wall. If that second trace hits, and if a floor check at the corner point finds ground to land on, bIsAtCorner is set and the corner prompt widget appears.

When the player presses the corner input, bWantsToGoAroundCorner is set in the input struct. The movement mode reads this flag and drives the character toward the corner point at CornerTransitionSpeed - bypassing the normal acceleration limiter so it’s instant rather than easing up over a second.

Gap movement was a later addition. At wall edges with no wall ahead, stepped perpendicular traces scan outward in GapStepSize increments looking for a coverable wall across open space. The first valid hit (with floor beneath it) becomes the gap target. Short gaps use a spin (character sidesteps), long gaps trigger a sprint (character runs face-first, rotating to face the travel direction mid-transit). Both are handled entirely within UCoverWalkingMode - no mode changes, no transitions.

Networking

Mover uses rollback-style network prediction. The client produces inputs, runs simulation locally, and sends inputs to the server. The server runs the same simulation with the same inputs. If the server and client disagree, the client gets corrected.

For cover to work in multiplayer, the server needs to make the same movement mode decisions as the client. That means the cover flags - especially bShouldBeInCoverMode - must travel through the replicated input collection, not just exist on the game thread.

The transitions handle this. Every simulation tick, UCoverEntryTransition::Evaluate_Implementation reads bShouldBeInCoverMode from FCoverModeInputs. If it’s true and the current mode is Walking, it returns the Cover mode name. Client and server both run this evaluation independently with the same input data, so they transition at the same tick.

Server-side validation in the transition independently traces to verify the claimed WallHitLocation has an actual wall there, and checks that the character isn’t suspiciously far from it. Requests that fail validation are rejected, leaving the client in Walking mode until a legitimate wall is found.

One networking issue worth noting: FCoverModeInputs has a lot of fields. 12 FVectors, 11 booleans, several floats. At raw serialization that’s around 1500 bits per struct instance. Mover bundles multiple input frames per RPC, and the total was exceeding the 16384-bit MaxNumBits limit.

The fix was to compress NetSerialize - booleans packed into a 32-bit flags field (11 bits), normals quantized to 16 bits per component, world locations truncated to integers. Compressed size is around 750 bits per instance, well within the limit.

Editor Visualization

The editor module adds a Cover Debug toggle to the viewport toolbar’s View Modes dropdown. When enabled, a subsystem scans static mesh surfaces near the editor camera every 0.5 seconds and applies a translucent overlay material:

  • Green - full cover
  • Yellow - half cover
  • Red - too low

It works with Nanite since it applies via material override on the mesh component rather than drawing geometry. Original materials are restored when the toggle is off.

What’s in the Plugin

  • UMoverCoverComponent - cover detection, wall tracking, corner/gap probing, widget management, event delegates
  • UCoverWalkingMode - cover movement mode with shimmy, depth correction, edge peeking, corner and gap driving
  • UCoverEntryTransition / UCoverExitTransition - network-safe mode transitions with server-side validation
  • FCoverModeInputs - replicated input struct with compressed NetSerialize
  • UCoverDebugSubsystem - editor cover surface visualizer
  • IA_Cover, IA_CoverCorner, IMC_Cover - preconfigured Enhanced Input actions and mapping context
  • Full Doxygen documentation with setup guide and screenshots

The plugin is compatible with any Mover-based character with no base class requirements. Tested on UE 5.8, packaged for 5.5 through 5.8.

Available on FAB: Mover Cover System

Support: phantomwiregames@gmail.com · Discord · Twitter
entry.summary: How I built a network-predicted cover system on Unreal Engine's experimental Mover plugin - wall classification, corners, gaps, a quaternion bug, and NetSerialize compression.

entry.title: Nightshift: From Getaway Driver to Elimination Circuit

link.title: Nightshift: From Getaway Driver to Elimination Circuit

entry.content:
Nightshift is a roguelite street racing tournament I’m building solo under my studio, PhantomWire Games. You start dead last, ranked #1000 out of 1000 in an underground elimination circuit. The routes are procedurally assembled every run, a perk draft between races lets you build your run identity, and every 100 ranks a named rival stands between you and the next tier. Think Hades meets Need for Speed Underground.

This is a breakdown of how it got here - from a scrapped prototype to a fully playable loop.

From Getaway Driver to Elimination Circuit

The project didn’t start here. It began in September 2024 as a Crazy Taxi-style getaway driver game - spawn into a procedural city at night, ferry criminals past police patrols before sunrise. That’s also where the name Nightshift came from. Early development was spent getting UE5’s Chaos Vehicle physics to actually feel right (suspension travel, tyre friction, centre of mass - it all has knock-on effects), while the open-world concept was prototyped alongside it.

By October 2025, it was clear the open-world getaway loop wasn’t tight enough - too much time navigating, not enough time doing anything interesting. The pivot stripped the game back to the part that was actually fun in playtesting: the racing itself. Roguelite structure went in on top - elimination tournament, perk drafts, procedural route assembly. The name stayed. The game became something far more defined.

Vehicles, Rendering & Art Direction

The visual identity draws from NFS Underground, Tokyo Xtreme Racer and Initial D. After testing several post-process approaches, I landed on a cel-shaded look built around the reverse hull technique - the same outline method Guilty Gear Strive uses - rendering an inflated, backface-only inverted mesh in black to get bold cartoon outlines with no post-process edge detection. Shadow regions use a halftone pattern for a printed, comic-panel feel.

Getting custom vehicles into a Chaos Vehicle project needs a specific bone hierarchy for wheels, axles and dampers, which is slow and error-prone to rig by hand. I built a Blender plugin that generates the full skeleton automatically from wheel placement alone, producing an FBX-ready rig every time. Vehicle paint runs entirely through a master material driven by a second UV channel mapped to flat colour regions on the body - no per-colour textures, full customisation (base colour, metallic finish, tint, decals) through material parameters alone. That system started life as a standalone university project and is being folded into Nightshift directly.

Race Framework & AI

The race loop runs on two UWorldSubsystems. URaceEventManager owns a six-phase state machine - Inactive → PreRace → Countdown → Racing → Finish → Results - broadcasting a delegate on every transition so any system can subscribe without coupling to the manager itself. Race position is resolved at 20hz using checkpoint count as the primary sort key and spline distance as the tiebreaker. URaceCheckpointManager handles wrong-way detection (velocity dot product against the checkpoint’s forward vector, debounced to avoid false positives when clipping a checkpoint at an angle) and keeps only the next two checkpoints visible at a time.

Racer AI follows a spline-following foundation with two layers on top: a lightweight vehicle avoidance pass that nudges racers around each other without full path replanning, and a utility-scored pickup system that evaluates race position, nearby threats, vehicle health and upcoming corner curvature every 1-2 seconds per racer to decide when to use an item - staggered so the whole field doesn’t pop an EMP in the same instant.

UI, HUD & the Perk Draft Loop

Perks run through the Gameplay Ability System as multipliers against a vehicle attribute set - speed, handling, acceleration, drift angle - so the system stays composable instead of a pile of one-off value overrides. On the design/UI side, I rebuilt the entire UI framework from the ground up so every menu and in-game widget shares a common base for focus management and input handling, which fixed a run of edge-case bugs (including one where the back-action prompt silently disappeared in certain menus).

The perk draft screen presents three cards after each race - name, rarity, icon and level, with the full description flipping open on hover. Crossing the finish line first shows your placement as big graffiti-style spray text rather than a plain number, before fading into a results table that correctly lists DNF racers instead of giving them a ghost time.

Selected perks save to the save game, level up if already owned, and get reapplied automatically - stats and HUD icons included - the next time you’re in a race. A SceneCaptureComponent2D feeding a HUD render target also drives a working rear-view mirror.

Scrapping the Open World

Before the current architecture, I built a full PCG pipeline for runtime open-world city generation - road network graphs, continuous race splines, the works. Once I properly stress-tested it in early 2026, the frame rate impact and level-streaming load times weren’t acceptable for a game that needs to feel fast and load a new run instantly. UE5’s Mass Traffic system was also evaluated for ambient vehicles and ruled out - too much integration overhead for what it was worth at this stage.

The call: no open-world city. Nightshift uses linear, procedurally assembled race routes instead - hand-crafted segments stitched together at runtime, closer to how F-Zero or Trackmania build a track than an open world. It’s a much better fit for a roguelite where every run needs to feel snappy, and it’s the kind of scope decision that’s easy to avoid making until it’s already expensive - better to find out in a stress test than six months into building systems on top of it.

Performance Engineering

Before building anything else on the rebuilt foundation, I put the project through a full optimisation pass. Disabling deferred rendering for DX11 forward shading (SM5) got a packaged build to 600-900fps at native 1440p on an RTX 3060 with a near-empty scene. Forward shading meant no Mega Lights support though, so I moved back to DX12 with hardware ray tracing enabled - about 0.5ms more frame time, but Mega Lights removes a large chunk of manual lighting work in a dynamic city environment. That build still held 400-500fps at native 1440p on desktop, and around 300fps at native resolution on a Steam Deck.

Where It’s At Now

Nightshift currently has a fully playable end-to-end loop: Title Screen → Garage Hub → Race → Results → Perk Draft → Garage Hub. It’s rough around the edges with placeholder assets throughout, but everything from here builds on a working foundation instead of a set of isolated tech tests. Rank progression, elimination logic and tying the tournament structure together end-to-end are next.

Read the full devlog series on PhantomWire
entry.summary: How Nightshift went from a Crazy Taxi-style prototype to a roguelite street racing tournament - vehicles, rendering, race framework, AI, UI, and the scope pivot that shaped it.

entry.title: How a mod I created for PAYDAY 3 made it into the base game

link.title: How a mod I created for PAYDAY 3 made it into the base game

entry.content:
When I first began working on VanillaHUD+, the goal was simple: improve Payday 3’s team HUD while staying true to its original visual language. The vanilla HUD at launch was clean but lacked clarity in certain areas. Information like crew ammo, tools, placeables and overkill status was missing - making teamwork unnecessarily harder as people would be forced to chat or use the chat wheel to ask for extra ammo.

I wanted to address that.

The Design Philosophy Behind VanillaHUD+

Working with an incredible concept artist from the community (FlamingFury1000), the vision behind VanillaHUD+ was to enhance readability, efficiency, and consistency, while keeping the aesthetic “vanilla-adjacent.” No flashy effects, no intrusive overlays—just cleaner layout logic and a focus on what matters during gameplay.

Some of the key changes I introduced:

  • Compact but rich player panels that emphasized key stats like renown level, ammo count, and equipment and overkill status.
  • Dynamic Heister Potraits that change whether the player is masked or unmasked
  • Hostage counter
  • Visual hierarchy tweaks to reduce clutter and boost legibility.
  • Performance optimisation by removing overused canvas panels.

What was introduced in patch 2.1.4

The official patch 2.1.4 arrived with changes that closely mirror many decisions from VanillaHUD+. With renown levels now showing, and the crewmates health and armor status being extended to also show ammo and equipment. The visual style with these changes are almost identical with VanillaHUD+ albeit some padding differences. The new update also introduced some very nice changes to the defeat states and downed counter which differ from VanillaHUD+. However, the dynamic heister potraits and overkill status seen in VanillaHUD+ are still missing from the base game.

Coincidence or Community Inspiration?

I don’t work at Starbreeze. I don’t have insider access. So I can’t say for certain whether my mod directly inspired these official changes.

But the similarities are striking.

It’s entirely possible that the Payday 3 team had similar goals, arrived at the same usability issues, and reached similar conclusions. Or—maybe—they saw what VanillaHUD+ offered and decided to integrate those ideas into the base game. Either way, it’s an encouraging sign.

This is what I love about modding. It’s not just a personal sandbox. It’s a dialogue. Sometimes, that dialogue loops back into the very games we love.

Technical Notes

VanillaHUD+ was developed using:

  • Figma
  • Unreal Engine 4.27
  • Custom Blueprint + UMG injections
  • Widget recreations from Uasset and Kismet Analysis

This project was not just a UI reskin - it required reverse engineering, hooking into HUD elements, and patching logic without breaking the core game loop. It was both a design and technical challenge.

What I Learned

This experience deepened my skills in:

  • UI/UX design for real-time games
  • Working within tight engine constraints
  • Respecting and extending a game’s original artistic direction
  • Creating tools and mods that are maintainable post-patch

It also reminded me that modding can be more than a hobby - it can be a form of prototyping, feedback, and design leadership.

Final Thoughts

Whether the similarities are coincidental or not, it’s incredibly rewarding to see a personal project align with an official design direction. If nothing else, it validates the design choices I made and reaffirms my belief in the power of player-driven iteration.

If you’re a developer, studio, or team interested in design-focused, technically capable talent - I’m currently open to opportunities. Let’s build better HUDs and UI, together.

Although it is now outdated, you can still view VanillaHUD+ mod on ModWorkshop

entry.title: Vehicle Customisation System: Journal
entry.content:
Master Material Setup

When it comes to handling the material of each mesh, I decided to set up a master material that is capable of handling all of the customisation options and their different properties. Using one master material is beneficial as it is more performant than just giving each mesh its own materials and reduces draw calls.

To achieve this, I researched how other games and programs handled similar things. I eventually stumbled upon UDIMs in 3D Modelling, which allow us to distribute UV islands across several textures. The process of having a UV offsetting system that assigns an image to specific UV tiles sounded something that was replicable in Unreal’s Material Editor. However instead of assigning an image, I opted to just assign colours to the UV tiles.

I started off by creating a material map mask that was split into 18 tiles. I chose 18 as that was the amount of different customisable options I planned for. This mask was made from the UV map in the meshes second slot, meaning all my meshes that will be using this master material will need a second UV map with the UVs arranged into the corresponding tiles.

After having the material map mask set up in Unreal, I created a basic template texture that was labelled with what each tile would affect. This would help when it comes to UVing the meshes to be compatible with the master material.

Now that I had the tile contents decided, I can create an atlas for selecting the tiles individually and applying a colour to them. Taking the horizontal and vertical map mask values, I subtracted the desired coordinate value and saturated the absolute value of that, then multiplied both the horizontal and vertical back together to get a successfully isolated tile. I could then multiply this tile with an input 4 vector.

Setting this up in a material function proved to be useful as it allowed me to be able to easily call the atlas multiple times in the future.

In the master material, I can now utilise this atlas function to assign colours and scalar parameters to the different tiles. I did this for the base colour, metallicness and emissivity of the material.

With the master material functional, I can now create material instances for the different meshes I import and can easily adjust the properties in the customisation system as it is all handled within one material.

Mesh UV Setup

To make sure that the different meshes worked correctly with the master material, they needed to be set up in a specific way. The process for this is quite simple and can be done by:

  1. Separating the meshes into the corresponding meshes (Body, Front and Rear Bumper, Hood, Side Skirts and Spoilers)
  2. For each mesh, create a new UV Map in the second slot. This will be the UV map that stores the UVs in the tiles they need to be in according to the material map mentioned above.
  3. For each tile, select the vertices/faces that should be placed in them, select the UVs and place them in the tile.
  4. Remove all existing materials and assign a single material to all vertices.

If done correctly, the meshes and UV map should look something like this, with all the required tiles being filled with the correct UV islands (Some are missing as the base mesh of this preview vehicle doesn’t have them).

Now this body and any kit meshes should be ready to import into Unreal Engine and can utilise the master material correctly.

Colour Selection

To be able to give the player a way of changing the part’s paint colour and metallicness, I needed to make some sort of colour selection menu. After researching how different photo editors and tools (like Photoshop or Blender or even Unreal Engine itself) handled colour selections, I had a rough idea of how I wanted to implement colour selection.

My initial concept was to have a ui widget, filled with a vertical gradient of the hue and a horizontal gradient of value, that had a thumb picker that allowed the player to pick the desired colour from the shown gradient. This would also have been ccompanied by a grid of recent colours to allow the player to have an easy way to reselect the same colours and match different parts if they wanted to.

However when it came to implementing this, I had some difficulty with setting up the colour picker so that it would read the colour under it. I first tried capturing the pixel under the picker to a render target and using the colour captured in the vehicle’s material. Although that did work in a sense, the colour it would capture would sometimes not be representative of the colour shown in the widget and also capturing the pixel to a render texture seemed a bit over engineered and not as optimised as I would want it to be.

So I went back to the beginning and chose to just use a HSV to RGB conversion to select the colour instead of a render texture. I tried converting the mouse’s position from absolute values to local values in the widget so that I can make the top left of the widget show as (0,0) and the bottom right to be (1,360). I needed to have the horizontal axis from 0-1 as this would be the value that would be used as the “value”. The vertical axis needed to be from 0-360 as this is what would be used for the “hue”. One of the issues I found while trying to implement this was that I lacked a way of getting a “saturation” value from this gradient texture. The final issue with this implementation that eventually made me change how it worked was that the mouse position wouldn’t always show the correct value depending on how the widget is used. If the widget was on its own and just added to the viewport, it worked fine. However if it was added to another widget as a userwidget, my calculations for converting the mouse positions to local space now become wrong and the colour is no longer correct as a result of this. I could have reworked the way I convert the mouse position and taken the different panels the widget can be nested into consideration, but I eventually decided that calculating the position on the gradient from the mouse position wasn’t a great solution. I wanted to create a more efficient widget.

After doing some much more needed research, I found the Unreal Engine has a pre-existing base widget that does everything I needed, the Synth2DSlider widget. This widget simply shows a sliding bar with a handle that allows the player to control the value between 0 and 1. As the slider widget itself has functions for getting the value of the handle/thumb, it means that I wouldn’t have to do any extra calculations or checking the mouse position. I did need to change the way the gradient was displayed as I was only using 0 to 1 values for the Synth2DSlider. I chose to take the same approach as Photoshop does and create a simple colour gradient that goes from white to the saturated colour on the horizontal axis and colour to black on the vertical axis. This allowed me to use the horizontal value of the thumb for the “saturation” in the HSV conversion and the vertical value of the thumb for the “value”. For the “hue”, I set up a second slider that could be used to adjust the value from 0 to 360, giving the player a full range of all the colours. This second slider would simply just adjust the “HUE” parameter I set up in the gradient material.

I also added a third slider that would control the metalness of the part. This is a simple 0-1 slider that would determine the metallicness of the part in the vehicle’s material. To save having to use multiple variables and functions, I take the value from the metalness slider and use that as the “alpha” of the HSV conversion. Although this means that the colours will sometimes not be visible if the metalness is full, that can simply be accounted for when displaying the colours as we just use a hard coded 1.0 value for alpha instead of the alpha in the current colour.

With the colour picker widget and the metalness now handled correctly, I had one thing left to implement. The recent colours grid. For this, I created a new button widget that closely resembled the concept button. This button would spawn whenever the colour picker changes colour. After getting this all working, I found a flow in the design of the recent colours grid. Even the smallest change (I.E a 0.01 value change in either of the values) would create a new recent colour button and the buttons would spawn as you are dragging the colours, essentially filling the whole grid with very similar colours with slightly different values. I added a threshold value change and also made it so that it only creates a new recent colour when you let go of the slider holder, applying the colour. In the end I wasn’t very happy with how it felt to use the recent colours. I found that if I changed too many colours while testing what looks nice, then a recent colour that I want to use would be replaced by another. Inevitably, I reworked the whole recent colour system and opted to do a favourite colours grid instead. This proved to be much more beneficial as it allowed the players to pick and choose their own common colours that they want to have easier access to. The current implementation only allows for seven favourite colours, however this can be adjusted in the future if needed.

Decal Editor

Another main feature of the vehicle system that I wanted to create was the ability to add vinyls and stickers, allowing the player to personalise their vehicles to the fullest. With the intention of making an editor for placing decals, I started by researching other racing games to see how they handled their customisations. I found that many of the games limited the customisation options in a way that I wanted to avoid, be that in the amount of decals a player can add or the placement being predefined locations on the vehicle. I took these limitations all into consideration and designed an editor that would be more accessible and allow for more creativity.

But to create an editor for decals, I first needed to set up decals. Luckily, Unreal Engine has a built in decal (actor or component) that projects a given material into the level. This was perfect for what I needed. Simply creating a decal material that projects a chosen texture worked well. However when it came to creating the material, I encountered an issue. I attempted to adjust the textures properties through the material to allow for rotating, scaling and recolouring the texture. The rotating and recolouring worked as intended. But scaling the texture too large would cause the texture to clip and cut off parts of the texture.

Initially, I tried working around the clipping by starting the texture at a scale of 0.75 and allowing the player to scale from a size between 0.5-1. This technically worked although I didn’t like the idea of limiting the scale size.

In the end, I chose to scale the decal component as a whole rather than just scaling the UV of the texture. This mitigated the clipping issue and removed the limited scaling size. Additionally at this stage of development, I also decided to keep the rotation logic inside the material rather than rotating the decal component, mainly as I wanted to be able to rotate the decal component in accordance to the location of the decal on the vehicle.

Now that I had the decal material and optional properties all decided and set up, I need a way of spawning the decals. As the main menu camera was dictated by a predefined sequence, I opted to have the player controller possess a new actor that handles a free camera that allows the player to orbit around the vehicle while placing the decals. Having an orbiting camera that can zoom, pan and rotate around the vehicle gives the player a lot of freedom with the decals placement. Once the player gets possession of this editor actor, a new decal is spawned. To calculate where the decal should be placed, a line trace is done every 0.1s from the mouse position to the middle of the screen and if the trace hits a vehicle then the decal gets moved to the hit position and is rotated using the hit normal vector to make sure the decal is facing the right direction.

To handle each individual decal, I created a primary data asset that stores the decals name and texture. Then I created a datatable that has a struct of category to decal data assets. This means that to add a decal to the game, all that needs to be done is import a texture, create a data asset for it and add it as a row to the data table and decide which category it should fall under. The widget that handles the picking of decals will read the data table and create a new category list for each unique category and a new button for each individual decal. I further optimised this decal creating process by creating an editor plugin that will automatically turn decal textures into data assets and automatically add them into the decal datatable. I dub this plugin, “Decal Maker”. On the click of the plugins toolbar button, it will read all textures in the /decal directory, check whether a data asset for it already exists and if not create a data asset then proceed to add the new asset to the data table. This speeds up the decal creating process as I no longer have to individually go through each texture making data assets for them and manually adding them to the data table. It simplifies the process down to importing all textures into its category directory in the /decals folder and clicking the plugins toolbar button. This however means that for the decal maker to work, the textures need to be named “T_Decal_[Category]_[Name]”.

Save and Loading

Now that the position, rotation, scale and colour can all be changed by the player and the editor works as intended, other than one minor caveat. Decals didn’t persist between sessions. As a matter of fact, no customisation options persisted. I needed to save the different customisations when modified and needed a way to load them. After creating a map of exactly what I was going to need to save, I created structs in the engine that followed the map and had each variable and created a new Unreal Save class that handled vehicles and customisations.

The save included an array of the top level struct “VehicleSave” which had the vehicle name, customisation options and vehicle data asset. This array can essentially be used as an “Owned” vehicles save which dictates what vehicles the player owns and allows for multiple vehicles of the same type but with different customisation options; each “VehicleSave” struct being a unique vehicle.

Evaluation

In this project, the main purpose and goal was to design and create a working vehicle customisation system. I chose to make this system as making it requires crucial planning and development skills that could be applied to making various other systems. I’m also a fan of racing games so it was something that was familiar to me. In the end, I’m proud that I was able to achieve what I set out to make and it works well. On a basic level, it works well as a concept or first version but I also acknowledge that it definitely needs some improvements and polishment before I would deem it “complete”.

After researching, I chose to make the project in Unreal Engine 5 because it was the game engine that I am most comfortable with and many companies are transitioning over to using Unreal Engine instead of in-house engines. Luckily the research I did on other racing and sim games that have customisation options was very helpful with creating a concept project that incorporates everything I had planned as I already had an idea of what was needed. Although I do wish that I had dedicated more time to playtesting the project when packaged as a few bugs appeared that didn’t show in editor. If I was to do this project again, I would know to test more vigorously and spend more time fixing issues. This has given me a better opportunity to see how a technical designer / system designer would work and what they would be responsible for. I feel like my work is closely up to par with what would be expected from a professional so I’m happy with how my project turned out.
